# What Is AI Governance?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-30 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI governance is how an organisation decides which AI uses are allowed, who owns them and how risk is checked. Three reference points dominate: the voluntary NIST AI RMF, the certifiable ISO/IEC 42001 management system standard, and the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations now apply from December 2027.

AI governance is the set of roles, policies, records and controls through which an organisation decides how it uses AI, who is accountable for each use and how risks are found and managed. Three frameworks shape most programmes: NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001 management system standard, and the EU AI Act. For a 20 to 500 person company, governance starts with an inventory, named owners and a record of decisions, not a committee.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What AI governance means

Governance answers four questions for every AI use: is it allowed, who owns it, how is it checked, and what is recorded. Policy documents are the visible part. The working parts are an inventory of AI systems, an owner for each, a risk classification, approval rules and evidence that the rules were followed.

| AI governance is | AI governance is not |
| --- | --- |
| Named owners and decisions for each AI use | A single ethics statement on the website |
| A risk-based inventory updated as tools change | A one-off procurement checklist |
| Evidence: approvals, logs, incidents, reviews | A tool that can be bought and switched on |
| Proportionate to the firm's size and exposure | A copy of a large bank's framework |

## The three reference frameworks

**NIST AI RMF.** NIST describes the framework as guidance for voluntary use by organisations designing, developing, deploying or using AI. Its core has four functions: govern (culture, roles and policy), map (context and risks of each use), measure (assessment and tracking) and manage (prioritising and acting on risks). A companion Playbook suggests actions for each. The Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, applies the framework to generative systems.

**ISO/IEC 42001.** The standard "specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving" an AI management system. It is intended for any organisation providing or using AI-based products or services. Like ISO 27001 for information security, it can be certified by an accredited body: BSI announced Dutch accreditation in December 2024, and UKAS granted its first UK accreditation for 42001 certification in January 2026.

**EU AI Act.** The Act is law, not guidance, and classifies AI uses by risk. Prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied from 2 February 2025, and general-purpose AI model rules from 2 August 2025. Article 50 transparency duties generally apply from 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and product-embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028.

| Framework | Type | Best used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NIST AI RMF and AI 600-1 | Voluntary US guidance | Structuring risk thinking for each use |
| ISO/IEC 42001 | Certifiable international standard | Showing customers a management system exists |
| EU AI Act | Binding EU regulation | Legal obligations by risk category |

> Governance is a record of decisions with owners, not a document that says decisions will be made.

## How a mid-size company starts

Large-enterprise programmes do not scale down well. **lowob**'s Gateway 0 asks for three decisions before any AI tool is bought, and the same logic gives a proportionate starting set.

| Step | What it produces | Framework link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory every AI use, including features inside existing software | A list with owner, purpose and data touched | NIST map; ISO 42001 scope |
| Classify by exposure | Client-facing, regulated or internal; check EU high-risk categories | EU AI Act risk tiers |
| Set the autonomy level per use | Answer, draft, act with approval, act and report, act alone | NIST manage |
| Name approvers and a kill switch owner | A matrix of who approves what | EU AI Act Article 14 oversight |
| Record decisions and outcomes | Reason, owner, status and expected outcome for each change | ISO 42001 documented information |
| Review quarterly | Updated inventory and incident list | NIST govern; ISO continual improvement |

For many mid-size firms, customer due diligence will ask for this list before any regulator does. A buyer's security questionnaire asking how AI is governed is answered by the inventory and the decision record, which is why **lowob** argues governance should start on the commercial line.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with the inventory.** Governance cannot cover AI uses nobody has listed.
- **Pick frameworks by purpose.** NIST for structure, ISO 42001 for certification, the AI Act for legal duties.
- **Check the dates.** EU high-risk obligations moved to December 2027 and August 2028.
- **Keep the evidence.** Owners, approvals and outcomes recorded are what governance looks like to an auditor.

## Next move

Ask each team lead to list the AI tools and features they use this week, including ones built into existing software. Give each line an owner; that list is the start of your governance record.
